maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. REID REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "NEW CANADIAN" OF FEBRUARY 28
PRIVILEGE-MR. REID REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "NEW CANADIAN" OF FEBRUARY 28
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of personal privilege affecting me as a member of parliament. On February 25 last, when the estimates of the Department of External Affairs were under discussion, in a speech expressing views concerning the Japanese in Canada differing from those expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), I made certain remarks which can be found at page 1020 of Hansard. In my remarks I pointed out that in my opinion the Japanese in Canada were an unassimilable race. Here are my exact words:
In answer to a question of mine it was admitted by Japanese that they owed allegiance first to Japan, and so long as every Japanese born here is registered in Japan -and is looked upon as a Japanese national he cannot be truly a Canadian. Hence my objection to -them as a class. They are not an assimilable race, and are different in their outlook from any other nationals in Canada.
This morning I received a copy of a newspaper called the New Canadian, published in Vancouver by the Japanese, in their own interests; and I am now going to read to the house an article which appeared in the issue of February 28, which contains a scurrilous personal attack upon both the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) and myself, which I do not intend to let go unchallenged. This is the statement:
Some rather caustic comments concerning Canadians of Japanese origin were bandied about in the House of Commons this week, in

War Expenditures Committee
a manner to suggest that several British Columbia members of the house are still unprincipled politicians, first, last and all the time.
Mr. A. W. Neill, the honourable member from Comox-Alberni, was once again the leading spirit in an attack upon the quality of our loyalty and our Canadianism. With due assistance from his companion in prejudice, Mr. Tom Reid from New Westminster, he sawed violently away at his favourite plank-one, by the way, that he has exploited to considerable advantage for many a year-"once a Jap, always a Jap."
With due deference to his prestige, his position and his fossilization, the editor of this weekly presumes to disagree. And with all respect to the honourable members, he publicly challenges Mr. Neill and Mr. Reid to an open debate to determine which proposition is the more valid:	"Once a Japanese, always a
Japanese," or "Once an oriental-baiting politician, always an oriental-baiting politician."
An agreement as to time, place or conditions may be deferred until the honourable members of the house have considered, with what means they have at their disposal, somewhat more pressing problems of Canadian unity and the Canadian war effort.
These statements are not only false; they are malicious, and I want to repudiate in the strongest possible terms this personal attack upon myself. At no time have I endeavoured to arouse hostile or racial feelings against the Japanese in British Columbia. It is true that I have endeavoured in this house to point out certain dangers which I believe exist in British Columbia or might exist if the franchise were granted the Japanese. I have also urged that control of our fisheries by the Japanese in British Columbia should not be permitted to continue. My statements, first that the Japanese are an unassimilable race and second that most if not all Japanese in this country, whether born in Canada or elsewhere, are registered in Japan as Japanese nationals, have never been refuted by anyone, not even the Japanese themselves.
Such a vilifying personal attack, Mr. Speaker, comes with poor grace from a race of people who have enjoyed, with the exception of the franchise, every phase of our Canadian social and economic life.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: By leave of the house, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) that the first report of the special committee on war expenditures, presented to the house yesterday, be now concurred in.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not rise for the purpose of dissenting from this report. Mr. Speaker, but there is one feature of it with regard to
which I think some explanation should be given. I refer to the matter of printing. The report contains a recommendation that so many copies of the proceedings in English and so many copies in French be printed at the discretion of the committee, which is quite unusual. I should like some explanation from the chairman as to why the committee desires to retain this discretion rather than have the usual resolution put through-simply an order of the house that the proceedings be printed.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the committee reserves to itself the right to determine from time to time whether its minutes and evidence shall be printed. It has been decided, until the committee determines otherwise, that the sessions of the committee shall be open sessions. If the committee should decide that in the interests of the nation its sittings shall be in camera, then the committee reserves to itself the right to determine whether the minutes and the evidence shall be printed. I suggest that that is a very proper reservation to make.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
While
concurrence in this report was granted by hon. members of the committee, nevertheless I think it ought to be pointed out that the motion for concurrence was carried on division.
With regard to the matter of printing, we know that a clause was inserted in the report now before the house providing that that matter should be left to the discretion of the committee. But I should like to reiterate the position I took on a previous occasion when the resolution was being considered, and to suggest that so far as possible all meetings of the committee should be general meetings, that the evidence not printed should be kept to a minimum and the maximum printed. I say this for the following reasons. The report asks concurrence in the proposal that the committee be empowered to divide itself into subcommittees, which subcommittees. in common with the committee itself, shall have power to call and examine witnesses, and so on. But, without thought of anything of a political nature-I am satisfied that no one serving on the committee is thinking of it in that sense at all-I must point out that the composition of the committee is such that it consists of only four members from His Majesty's Loyal Opposition, one member from the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and one from the Social Credit group. That leaves a committee on which there are eighteen members of the government party. In reply to an observation from the other side I will add "in charge of that committee." I hope, Mr. Speaker, that they realize they are in charge, and will not dominate the committee.

Royal Canadian Mounted Police
I hope they will leave their domination on the doorstep before they come in, and remember that while we are at war we are going to look at this matter from a big, broad point of view, to help the present situation.
But coming to the point I want to emphasize, those four members are anxious to study the problems which come before the committees-

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: So are we.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
-in common with their fellows on the committees. Four members cannot sit on five committees; therefore I suggest that the main evidence be taken and the main portion of the work conducted by the general committee. In like manner a maximum of the evidence should be printed, for the added reason that all hon. members will want to know what is going on, and the only way they can know is by their reading of the printed record. And, more important than the membership of this house, Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada will want to know what is going on.
With all due respect to those who have cast reflections upon some of the members of the fourth estate who occupy seats up above us, they are perhaps even better fitted than we are to inspire public confidence and to remind Canada that we are at war. We look forward to the press doing a real job of encouraging our people in their war effort, and of reminding those in Canada who are not thinking about a war that there is a war on.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: LETTER REFERRED TO BY MEMBER FOR NORTH BATTLEFORD ON MARCH 5

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LETTER REFERRED TO BY MEMBER FOR NORTH BATTLEFORD ON MARCH 5
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday of last week, March 5, the hon. member for North Battleford (Mrs. Nielsen) read a letter, or part of one, which she had received from James L. Hatton, of North Battleford. Subsequently the letter was laid on the table of the house. In it there were statements which cast rather damaging reflections on the Royal Canadian Mounted Police-

subtopic: LETTER REFERRED TO BY MEMBER FOR NORTH BATTLEFORD ON MARCH 5
speechtext: What about the latter part of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LETTER REFERRED TO BY MEMBER FOR NORTH BATTLEFORD ON MARCH 5
speechtext: -and its work in that locality. In fairness to the force, and as the high repute of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is one of the most valuable assets in Canada, I wish to lay on the table of the house a statement dated March 10, 1941, signed by the same gentleman, which has been given to the inspector in charge of the mounted police in that part of Saskatchewan. The statement is countersigned by the inspector.

subtopic: LETTER REFERRED TO BY MEMBER FOR NORTH BATTLEFORD ON MARCH 5
speechtext: Read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LETTER REFERRED TO BY MEMBER FOR NORTH BATTLEFORD ON MARCH 5
speechtext:
I have no objection. It is as follows:
James L. Hatton, auctioneer, states as follows:
Inspector Spriggs has to-day shown me a copy of a letter which I wrote to Mrs. Dorise Nielsen, M.P., on the 25th of February, 1941. I recognize this letter as a true copy of the one which I wrote.
At paragraph (3) of this letter I stated that I had had a conversation with Sergeant Hill on the 22nd and that he had stated the following:
"The-

Trans-Canada Air Lines
I am sure the house will excuse me if I do not repeat the two following words-
-can't she see that the same law will put her behind the wires, whether she believes it or not, and believe me she'll be there before long if she keeps up the pace she's hitting for they'll frame up something somehow either under the 5th Column or agitation against the war effort or disloyalty.
She should remember she's not a lawyer and she may leave a loophole somewhere and if she ever does in she goes. I'd imagine she should be able to see that she can do a lot more good by having her freedom than in an internment camp for the duration. Of course if she wishes to become a martyr to the cause she can be one by being interned, but I fail to see what she can ever gain by that. First thing she knows she'll be down there keeping Houde of Montreal company."
The foregoing statement in quotation marks embodies the full contents of what I had personally in my own mind and unfortunately, I quoted it as having been made by Sergeant Hill, believing it would have more weight and make a greater impression than it would have made on Mrs. Nielsen had I been expressing my own thoughts. The most important feature of the whole letter was to make her realize the seriousness of the attitude she is now taking towards the defence of Canada regulations during the war. This letter was absolutely a confidential letter and has been exposed to the public without the consent of the writer who had no intention in his mind of being disloyal or causing friction anywhere at any time other than between Mrs. Nielsen and himself. I deeply regret that my confidence has been betrayed, at a time when I thought I was giving confidential advice as to her better conduct in the future.
The actual conversation which took place between myself and Sergeant Hill on the 22nd of February, last, was dealing with newspaper articles in which Mrs. Nielsen had been reported as having taken up the part of persons who had been interned. Sergeant Hill was pointing out to me the impossibility of trial by jury in these cases, he -said that such procedure would be applicable in peace time but not in war. However he did not make any definite statement such as I have embodied above in quotation marks. I personally considered Mrs. Nielsen to be going too close to the border line and taking too much of a chance of overstepping or making some statement under which she might be charged as a fifth columnist or as an agitator or even for disloyalty.
As a result of my conversation I thought this matter over very carefully for a couple of days and decided that if I could make Mrs. Nielsen think that these things came from some one in authority she might take them more seriously and perhaps change her attitude as a result, and nut her support back of something that would be of vast importance towards the winning of the war or the relieving of distress where it was needed.
This statement has been given voluntarily by me without any pressure having been brought to bear from any quarter, and it is still my opinion that Mrs. Nielsen should change her attitude towards the war and the defence of Canada regulations.
J. L. Hatton.
Witness:
F. E. Spriggs,
Inspector.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES MONTREAL-MONCTON-HALIFAX MAIL SERVICE- HALIFAX ON MAIN TRANSCONTINENTAL AIR ROUTE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES MONTREAL-MONCTON-HALIFAX MAIL SERVICE- HALIFAX ON MAIN TRANSCONTINENTAL AIR ROUTE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I desire to direct a question to the Postmaster General. In view of the important part that the port of Halifax is playing in Canada's war effort, may we hope at an early date for an improvement in the air mail service out of Halifax?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES MONTREAL-MONCTON-HALIFAX MAIL SERVICE- HALIFAX ON MAIN TRANSCONTINENTAL AIR ROUTE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) was kind enough to give me notice of his intention to ask this question. I would advise him that with the concurrence of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) I have pleasure in stating that the Trans-Canada air mail service will be extended on or about April 15 from the former eastern terminal at Moncton, New Brunswick, to Halifax, and that the frequency of service between Montreal, Moncton and Halifax will be increased to two round trips daily including Sunday. This will furnish a direct air mail service between Halifax and Vancouver, and by eliminating the necessity of a transfer of
Trans-Canada Air Lines

mails and passengers at Moncton will further reduce the elapsed time necessary to fly between the Atlantic and Pacific shores of this dominion. The inclusion of Halifax on the main transcontinental air route is the logical outgrowth, not only of the continually increasing volume of air mail destined for and originating in Halifax, but also of the progressive policy of the Post Office Department in furnishing Canadians the best possible air mail service, an air mail service second to none.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES MONTREAL-MONCTON-HALIFAX MAIL SERVICE- HALIFAX ON MAIN TRANSCONTINENTAL AIR ROUTE
speechtext:
May I
inquire as to the type of equipment that will be used in carrying out this extended air service?
Hon. ANGUS L. MacDONALD (for the Minister of Transport): May I say that it is proposed to put on the route from Moncton to Halifax the regular type of plane used in other parts of the Trans^Canada service; that is, Lockheed planes, each with ten seats. The Postmaster General has already stated that there will be two planes a day in to and out of Halifax. I might add that the exact date when this service will commence is not known at the moment to the officials of the Department of Transport because there are stall certain works to be performed on the air field near Halifax, but there is every indication that the estimate given by the Postmaster General will prove correct. I think that before the end of the month of April this service will be in operation.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES MONTREAL-MONCTON-HALIFAX MAIL SERVICE- HALIFAX ON MAIN TRANSCONTINENTAL AIR ROUTE
speechtext: Is it the intention that the regular Trans-Canada air liners shall continue to have their terminus at Moncton, or will they proceed to Halifax? Will there be what is known as a taxi service between Moncton and Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES MONTREAL-MONCTON-HALIFAX MAIL SERVICE- HALIFAX ON MAIN TRANSCONTINENTAL AIR ROUTE
speechtext:
I am not able to answer that question definitely. The objection hitherto from the point of view of Halifax has been that planes running from Moncton to Halifax were only six-seater planes and consequently there was a good deal of congestion. Sometimes as many as twenty to twenty-five passengers might want to take the plane, and with the six-seater plane making only one or two flights a day a number of passengers were unable to get accommodation.
The great desire of the people down there was not that Halifax should be the terminal but that some arrangement should be made whereby the congestion at Moncton might cease and passengers from Montreal and points west be assured of accommodation.

subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO RECENT FLYING ACCIDENTS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of National Defence for Air):
speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO RECENT FLYING ACCIDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of
the recent series of unfortunate flying accidents, I think it is advisable to make a statement to this house. The following particulars are available concerning the three fatal accidents which occurred yesterday at No. 8, Service Flying Training School, Moncton; No. 4 Service Flying Training School, Saskatoon and No. 31 Air Navigation School, Port Albert, in which eleven personnel were fatally injured, two seriously injured and one uninjured and six Anson aircraft were destroyed.
Moncton. Two aircraft on a normal formation flight practice interlocked at 2,000 feet. In one aircraft with a crew of three on board, two pilots were unable to abandon the aircraft and crashed with it, killing one and seriously injuring the other whilst the third pupil pilot abandoned by parachute and landed safely. The other aircraft broke away after collision and fell straight down killing the only pilot on board.
Port Albert. Two Anson aircraft took off at a fifteen minute interval on separate exercises approximately in the same direction. The weather was clear everywhere. They came into collision, and it appears one knocked the tail off the other and both aircraft crashed out of control. The aircraft w'ere flown by experienced staff pilots. Seven of the occupants of the two Ansons were killed and the wireless operator, the only one to survive, was seriously injured. From evidence at hand it is considered that they may have been blinded by the sun on a turn. Why they were at the same place and height is unknown.
Saskatoon. Two Anson aircraft were on a normal formation flight. One overtook the other and collided. Both aircraft disintegrated in mid-air at 3,000 feet, killing both pilots. All the above accidents were on normal routine training flights. No evidence of mechanical failure is considered likely.
Accidents during 1940. The following accidents occurred during the first year of operation of the British commonwealth air training plan:
Fatal-25.
Tniured-33.
Total-267.
Hours flown-233,056.
Total accident rate-1-10 per thousand hours.
Fatal accident rate-0-11 per thousand hours.
Only 32 schools were in operation during this period, that is from April 1 to December

Air Force-Flying Accidents
31, but the 233,056 hours flown indicates the intensive training which was canned out. During this period the accident rate per 1,000 hours flown was:
Fatal accidents-0-11 per thousand hours.
Injured accidents-0-14 per thousand hours.
Uninjured accidents-O'94 per thousand hours.
Total accidents-1-19 per thousand hours.
Out of the total of 267 accidents which occurred during 1940, the major number was caused through normal errors of pupils during flying training, such as (a) not being able to correct a swing on landing; (b) carelessness in taxi-ing; (c) faulty manipulation of ancillary controls. Nine accidents occurred through collision in the air, which in most cases can be attributed to either bad weather or lack of vigilance by the aircraft crews.
No aircraft of any particular type used in training has revealed itself to be more prone to accidents than any other type, and in comparison with the flying hours carried out, the rate of accidents per hours flown was found to be not abnormal.
Accidents have increased during the first month of 1941, that is in January, as follows: total serious and minor accidents, 163 (18 deaths); flying hours carried out, 99,460; accident rate, 1-6 per 1,000 hours.
The flying time of 99,460 hours during the one month of January 1941 is very nearly 50 per cent of the total flying carried out during 1940 and the accident rate of 1-6 compares with the 1-19 of 1940.
I have not worked out the fatal accident rate for the month of January.
With respect to the action taken for the prevention of accidents:
1.	Air regulations are promulgated by the Royal Canadian Air Force to cover regulations which affect all schools throughout the service and flying orders are promulgated by each station for local regulations affecting their own locality only. One copy of air regulations is issued to each qualified pilot and one to each two pupils. These regulations cover such things as: minimum altitude at which aerobatics are carried out, the operation of aircraft on cross country flights, forced landings, restrictions imposed on various types of aircraft, low flying, et cetera.
2.	Courts of inquiry. Courts of inquiry are held on all accidents of a serious nature, the courts being composed of qualified officers who thoroughly investigate all circumstances surrounding the accident. The court makes findings and recommendations to prevent a recurrence. The findings and recommendations
of the court of inquiry are fully considered by command headquarters and in turn by Royal Canadian Air Force headquarters who take the appropriate action on the recommendations and findings.
3.	Analysis of flying accidents. Each command is required to make a summary analysis of each accident quarterly. This quarterly analysis of accidents is circulated within the command and all pilots must initial as having read and understood.
4.	Syllabus of flying instruction. Pupils are given individual instruction in the air by their flying instructor in aerobatics and spinning, to enable them to be fully conversant with the methods of recovering from any unusual altitude which they may inadvertently get into. They are also given instruction in low flying which is limited to dual only, and the importance of keeping a continuous lookout in the air.
5.	Syllabus of ground instruction. Syllabus of instruction at flying training schools require the chief instructor to give lectures based upon the analysis of flying accidents to all pupils under training. The chief instructor gives details of the causes of these accidents and explains in detail to the pupils steps which they should take to guard themselves against being involved in any accident.
6.	Posters. All flying training schools are supplied with a number of posters to bring home forcibly to the pilots the serious effects which result from disregard of air regulations, which have been brought into effect as the result of many years' experience. New posters are in the course of production.
7.	All possible steps are taken to prevent accidents, both in the air and on the ground, but in spite of these precautions accidents still occur. A large proportion of them are due to the human element for which it is impossible to legislate.
May I add that repetition of such accidents is far from making us callous. Indeed we view with the utmost anxiety the great loss of life involved in these accidents, and we shall continue by every means in our power to try to protect these young men not only against unforeseen occurrences but in many cases against their own carelessness.

subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO RECENT FLYING ACCIDENTS
speechtext: May I take advantage of this question to place on Hansard a comparison with the training figures of the Royal Air Force in Great Britain? During the months of July and August, 1940, which are regarded as good flying months, there were 66 deaths in the Royal Air Force during 293,700 hours of flying. speechtext: I do not believe that the minister quite understood what I was driving at. A plane which is up for an hour with five men in it represents an equivalent of five passenger hours as against one hour of flying time for the plane. I wish to be certain as to what the minister intended. It makes a very great difference in the percentages.

speechtext: I desire to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture. In view of the statement made last night by Major Tisdall, nutrition expert and adviser on nutrition to the Department of National Defence, as to the necessity of providing vitamin B-l in flour as a means of preserving vitality, will the minister take the necessary steps to see: (1) that this type of bread only is supplied to our fighting forces, and (2) that only flour containing this vitamin is exported to Britain during the war?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION OF VITAMINIZED FLOUR AND FLOUR PRODUCTS
speechtext: I listened to the address last evening of Major Tisdall and also the address which followed, delivered by Mr. Newman, of the cereals branch of the Department of Agriculture. speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, March 13, consideration in committee of a resolution to provide sums not exceeding §1,300,000,000 for the year ending March 31, 1942, for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war.-Mr. ILsley- Mr. Fournier (Hull) in the chair.
War Appropriation Bill

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Just prior to adjournment last evening I was speaking of the importance of making the best use of our available tonnage. I had pointed out that, owing to insufficient harbour facilities, there had been a serious congestion of shipping at the port of Saint John this winter, and that this was delaying our war effort. I had pointed out, further, that the national harbours board held a meeting in January in the city of Saint John when this problem was considered. I was about to say, when the house adjourned, that I had read in the press recently that the government proposes, in order to assist in relieving this congestion, to build a timber wharf, a trestle wharf I believe it is to be, about nine hundred feet long, this wharf to be ready when the winter port opens next autumn. That is a step in the right direction; it will improve the situation, but unfortunately it will not, in my opinion, fully meet the need. The representations made by the city of Saint John to the national harbours board should be carried out. I should like the Minister of Munitions and Supply or the government to tell us just what steps they have in mind to improve the situation at the port.
At the port of Saint John we have the wharves; we have the longshoremen and we have the railway connection. I understand that last summer some ports in the country were congested, but the port of Saint John was more or less vacant during the greater part of the summer. In order to prevent congestion in other ports in Canada and to facilitate the dispatch of cargoes of war materials and supplies overseas, I urge the government to consider the advisability of using the port of Saint John to a greater extent during the coming summer.
In conclusion, I would again urge the government to take a broad and statesmanlike view of the manner in which our war expenditures for manufacturing plants are to be made, and to take advantage of the opportunity that I believe is now presented to it of implementing, to some degree at least, the Rowell-Sirois report by improving the financial and economic position of the maritimes through the establishment this year in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia of war industries which will have a possibility of surviving as peace time industries after victory has been achieved. Out of the amount of 8307,000,000 that is being advanced to build industrial plants in this country, the very small sum of $182,526 has been spent in New Brunswick. This is not good enough.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
In connection with the
statement which was made to the committee earlier in the week by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), I think it would be well if either he or the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Gardiner) would give us a more detailed explanation with regard to the calling up of young Canadians for training under the National Resources Mobilization Act, and also with regard to the whole compulsory training scheme.
There is much doubt, much uncertainty, and I think much bewilderment in the minds of the Canadian people about the present method of calling up our young Canadians and about the compulsory training scheme. The time has come when the ministry should tell the committee and the people the purpose of this compulsory training. Let us know the aim of the government in connection with this whole scheme. For example, is it to give all our man-power a short period of training, or is it to train men for the reserve army, or is it to obtain recruits for the active army, or is it for some other purpose? My point is that the government should make some clear-cut statement as to the purpose so that the Canadian people will know. There are thousands and thousands of these young men who are vitally interested, and more thousands of their relatives who are also interested, and there is great general interest across the country in the purpose of the scheme.
Last summer, when the blitzkrieg struck and France was falling the Canadian parliament enacted the National Resources Mobilization Act; a few weeks after its enactment we were told, if I remember correctly- and if I am wrong in any of my points I would ask to be corrected by one of the ministers as I go along-that the purpose of the compulsory training was to give all the man-power in Canada preliminary military training. I think we were told that about
300,000	Canadians ranging in age from twenty-one to forty-five years would be given training for a period of thirty days. I also understood that another purpose was to provide a force which could be used for the defence of Canada. There were to be practically no exemptions from this training with the exception of the Doukhobors, the Men-nonites and perhaps one or two other classes.
When the house met in November Canada had had two or three months' experience with the plan, and I think it will be admitted

War Appropriation Bill
that it had then developed that there was no real tie-up with the fighting forces. For example, all the young men who received the training were posted to reserve army units, but merely by having their names included on the roster, in other words, the names were on the rolls, but the young men were not actually taking part in the work of the reserve army unit to which they were attached. Further, that reserve army unit could not recruit them into its ranks if it wanted to. I believe that until some time in January the reserve units were not allowed even to recruit the young men who had been posted to them.
Further there was no chance, or very little, given to these young men to join the active army; recruiting was not open; no facilities were provided for them to get into the active army if they wished to do so. I understand that they were asked whether they were willing to serve in the active army, but that was as far as it went. I believe, further, that the navy and the air force took steps to go into the camps, or set up recruiting stations near the camps, and did their best to persuade the young men to join their respective forces. The active army, however, refused to do that; it made no attempt whatever to get these young men into the ranks. Many of these young men who took the month's training went back into civil life.
The training was, of course, very short, and I think the house was unanimous in the belief that, to be effective, the training should be extended. In November, the Minister of National Defence announced that the period of training would probably be extended to four months, and that is now to be done.
But the position is far from clear. The government has decided that twenty-one year old men are to be called up, and I understand that the exemptions are to be wider than when the men were being called for the thirty days' training.
The present scheme is not entirely fair to these young men of twenty-one. During the period between the adjournment of the house in December and the reopening of the session in February, I heard many expressions of opinion to that effect. I think these young men feel they are being picked on. They find difficulty when they apply for work. Prospective employers ask their age; and when they find that the men will soon be twenty-one, the answer is, "Well, we don't want you. You are going to be twenty-one in a short time and you will be taken away from the job, so we will not take you on." Many of these young men are sons of men who served in the last war. It just so happens that setting this age at twenty-one means that 14873-98
a great many of the sons of men who served in the last war are included. The young men feel that if the call should come for men to fight, they, having been trained, will be chosen. I believe they are just as willing to serve as anyone else, but there is the feeling that the burden should be spread over a larger number of shoulders.
Will the Minister of National Defence or the Minister of National War Services explain whether the intention is that, after these young men have had their training, they should go back into civil life, or is it intended that they should go into the forces? I ask the ministem to inform us now as to the aim of the government in this regard. If the aim is to obtain as many recruits as possible for the active fighting forces, then I suggest that the government should go all-out to persuade these young men to enlist in the active army. Give them every possible facility for getting into that force. If it is also desired to build up an army for the defence of Canada, it does seem to me that other steps should be taken than those in contemplation at the present time. If the plan is to build up an army' for the defence of Canada, why not put these men into the active army, for service in Canada only, after they are trained? Under the terms of the National Resources Mobilization Act they can be called only to serve in Canada. Why should they not be put into the active army on that basis? We need many trained men to defend our shores should such defence be necessary, and it is far better to have too many than too few. At the present time I doubt whether we have a sufficient number of trained men in Canada for our defence, should an attempt be made at invasion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does my hon. friend mean an attempted invasion of Canada?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes. If some step such
as I suggest is taken; if these men are put into the active army-I do not suggest that this should apply to the men now under call but rather it should apply to those who attend future camps-I think the government should choose from a much wider age group, and that such choice should be made by lot, by much the same method as is being followed in the United States at present. I believe also that much wider exemptions should be granted. Where men are needed in industry; where men are needed at home, they should be exempted from service. The main thing is that the government should announce whatever policy it has, now, or just as quickly as possible, in order that the people of Canada may see the picture and may know at what we are aiming. If

War Appropriation Bill

that is done, the government will get far more understanding and far greater support across the country than it is getting at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Most of the questions raised by the hon. gentleman have to do with the Department of National Defence, and, I am sure, will be dealt with by my colleague, but perhaps I might answer that part having to do with the Department of National War Services.
We are asked to call out the necessary number of men to make up the camps. It has been estimated that the twenty-one year old group, together with those who were called for the thirty-day training but had their training postponed for one reason or another, will be sufficient to cover at least a considerable part of the present year. For that reason the first call has gone out for approximately six thousand men of the twenty-one year old group; that is, those who have become twenty-one since July 1 last and those who were twenty-one before last July but who did not train in any camp during the previous year.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is, those whose training was postponed?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes. As has been indicated, the first call has been issued to these men, who will report to a medical practitioner for examination, just as the men did under the thirty-day plan.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Before the minister goes on to deal with the medical examination, would he be good enough to enlighten me with respect to one point. Which department determines the category to be called? Is it his department or the Department of National Defence? That is to say, who determines whether only the men of twenty-one will be called? Is that the prerogative of his department or of the Department of National Defence?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The decision to call those of twenty-one years of age was based largely upon an examination of the records by both departments in order to obtain the number required to fill the camps that are being set up by National Defence, starting with those twenty-one years of age for the first call. Then the medical examiner determines whether the man is in a category which would require him to report to the camp. The individual has then the right to apply, not for exemption but for postponement, to the board at the centre of the military district, and, if necessary, the board may require the individual to appear in person to be examined in connection with his suggestion that his training should be postponed.
TMr. Green.]
I do not know that it is quite correct to say that the groups whose training is to be postponed have been enlarged. It is just possible that reasons for postponement will be accepted now that were not accepted for the shorter course. At the moment I would not care to go further than that. Two or three days ago, I think, I said that the regulations would be laid on the table before the end of this week. The only reason why they have not been laid on the table is that they were referred to the Department of Justice, which just finished looking over them to-day. As a result, some changes in phraseology have to be made, but I am hopeful that we shall have them by Monday or, at the latest, Tuesday of next week. Therefore, at the moment I should prefer not to go into detail with regard to certain matters as to which I have not seen the final phraseology. Generally speaking, however, the postponements will be for reasons similar to those under the thirty-day training, giving consideration to the fact that persons will have to be away from home or from places of business for four months instead of thirty days. So far as agriculturists are concerned, or those who have seasonal employment, some concessions will be taken into consideration. For example, agriculturists will not be compelled to go to camp under the first call, or, I would say, under the second call; but they will be expected to go for the third four months' period, which will be in the winter months of next year.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What is going to be done in the case of the dairy farmer?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: A choice will be given. Of course it is not compulsory that one who is in one of the seasonal employments should remain out of camp in the summer months. If he desires to go to camp in the summer, in order to avoid having to go in the winter months,' he will be permitted to do so. I should imagine there would be some divisions in families as to whether they prefer certain groups to come at one time or at another, although it is not likely there would be more than one in the twenty-one year old group. In that group, however, there might be a hired man as well as a member of the family.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I have in mind an actual case which came to my attention. This was the case of a widow with only one son, who was twenty-one years old and had been called. As it happens, he was milking twenty-one cows. She and her son came to my office during the recess, and appeared to be greatly perturbed over the situation. I told her what I thought was the

War Appropriation Bill
position. I said that I believed he could get a postponement, but that sooner or later he would have to go, and that the mother would have to hire somebody to take his place. She then pointed out the difficulty of securing help on the farm, on account of the fact that so much labour was being attracted by the work going on at that season of the year in various communities in the province.
My point is that in a case like that there ought to be some provision for selectivity, and that that boy ought not to be called at all. I advised the young man, however, that I thought the four-months' period of training was approaching, and that he might be wise to go to camp. I believe he did so. I do not know whether the mother milked the cows, or what happened. Possibly this was an extreme case, but certainly it was one where the boy should not have been called, under present circumstances. That is one of the weaknesses of the scheme. There is no provision for selectivity, and I am reminded by my colleagues that the case I have described could be duplicated in many instances throughout the length and breadth of the land. The minister would not be doing any violence to the condition he has set up if that sort of thing were considered. Having regard to the number of twenty-one year old men available, I am satisfied that that young man ought not to be called, or, in any event, at least not until later.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Before the last call was made under the thirty-day plan, and at a time when the four-months' plan was under consideration, a letter went out signed by myself as Minister of National War Services, after consultation with the government, to the effect that in cases such as the one now described the board could give special consideration for the last thirty-day period, in view of the fact that the whole plan might be changed, in which event we would probably be giving consideration to regulations of a different kind. I imagine a number of cases were dealt with during the last period on that basis.
Under the new regulations, while it has not been provided that anyone can be exempted, it is set out that consideration should be given in cases of hardship. As I understand it, there is a hardship clause in the British conscription measure.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: And in the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes, and in the United States. We have attempted to write the same principle into our regulations, despite the fact that our law is not a conscription law, in the sense that the others are. We are, however, having them appear before the 14873-98J
board. That is, the individual must make application before the board, and indicate his desire that special consideration be given his case. Having made that application, while he would not be exempted his case would be postponed, and he would be subject to call from time to time, or as conditions might change. In that event he would probably be called up, or from time to time he would be asked whether his condition had changed. What happened would depend somewhat upon the circumstances surrounding any particular case.
So far as groups are concerned, it is the present intention that industrialists should make application in a manner somewhat similar to that in which they applied under the thirty-day plan, if they desire to have a group in their plant considered for postponement, either because they are keymen or because they are taking part in an industry where it is essential that, for the time being, the staff ought not to be disturbed. Again, in this instance postponements would be allowed.
But postponements under the present regulations are not limited to twelve months; they can be made for a longer period. The thirty-day plan postponements were all confined to the twelve-months period.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Within
twelve months.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes; within twelve
months they were called again. But postponements made under the present regulations extend beyond that.
These men report to camps, and after they have reported and have passed medical examinations in the camps they are entirely in charge of the Department of National Defence.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: As I understand it, since the training has been extended to a four-months period, under the present basis of utilizing man-power there will be a sufficiency of young men attaining the age of twenty-one years, and the call will never go beyond the twenty-one year old class. Am I correct in my understanding?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That has been stated.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, in the press.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There is not a sufficient number of young men of the twenty-one year old class-at least, I do not believe there is-when we take into consideration those whose participation will be postponed either on account of their connection with industry, or because of training they may be following
War Appropriation Bill

in universities, which may be considered of as much importance as other training, or for other reasons. Taking all matters into consideration, I would doubt that there would be enough young men in the twenty-one year old class to make up the 6,000 a month.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
For four
months.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Six thousand are called' every month until we get to 24,000, and then
6.000	go in and 6,000 come out, which means that we call 72,000 over the year. I doubt very much if, in the result, there would be
72.000	available out of some 96,000 of that age group.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Is 96,000 the total number of the twenty-one year old
class?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
About 96,000 is the
number in the twenty-one year old class. We must consider the percentage turned down because of physical condition, others whose cases may be postponed because they are engaged in certain important industries, others who have joined the forces voluntarily, and who are of that age, and others who are taking training in some acknowledged military school. Therefore it is just possible that there may not be enough in the twenty-one year old class to carry right through the year.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: How many will become twenty-one years of age in each year?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Approximately the same number that are in the year age group called up. There may be a few more or a few less, but it would be about 96,000.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
At the time the new programme was announced, it was stated in the press that enough men would be found in the twenty-one year old group, and that it would not be necessary at any time to go beyond that group. As a result of that press statement, there was a feeling in many quarters that some other basis for selecting these men ought to be found. It was considered that it was not fair always to insist that the twenty-one year old men must break into what they were doing and take their training, and that the men of twenty-two, twenty-three or twenty-four years should go scot-free for the duration of the war. It was contended that if there are sufficient young men in the twenty-one year old class to keep the training scheme in operation, then a hardship would be suffered by those in that age group, and that the result would be that no responsibility would be placed on other young men at other ages.

I suggest to the minister that if, as the programme progresses, he finds that only the twenty-one year old men are going to be called, and that the men in that class will be available in sufficient numbers to fill the requirements, the government ought to give consideration to working out some other basis of selection. It might be done by lottery, as it is done in the United States, or on some other basis. Otherwise only the twenty-one year old men in Canada will have training, and the other young men in other age groups will not be compelled to take that training.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
If the war were not going on year after year and a system of this kind were established, we could say that probably only the twenty-one year age class would be called up. If we kept calling out the twenty-one year age class and then sent them home after four months, in ten years every one between the ages of twenty-one and thirty would have received training. I do not, however, anticipate that this will be the condition. I may say that the announcement made to the press was not to the effect that the twenty-one year age group would be the only group called; it was to the effect that if there were sufficient men in the twenty-one year age class, that would be the only class called; if it were necessary to go beyond that class in order to obtain a sufficient number of men, that would be done. The twenty-one year age class was the only one mentioned, but I think it will be found that the wording was sufficiently broad to cover what I am saying.
Men are enlisting continuously, and it is just possible that if 25 per cent of the twenty-one year age group should enlist, there would not be enough men to fill the camps. They might enlist in the air force, the navy or somewhere else. As we go on with the war, it may become more and more necessary to take in the higher age groups in order to fill the camps if we are going to continue to have four months training. I should not like it to be understood that it is definitely decided that we are going to call for training only those in the twenty-one year age group. The intention is to start with that group and continue calling them as long as we need men for the camps.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Is it the
intention of the government to take a larger body of men? Are the facilities to be extended so that they can take more than 6,000 a month as time goes on?

speechtext:
Is it the intention to train
72,000	men a year, or will there have to be deducted from that total those who are found to be unfit after having been called up?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: A minute ago the minister mentioned that there were some industrial training schemes which took men from under the National Resources Mobilization Act. What are those training schemes?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The Minister of Labour has some schools which are operating to train men for certain lines of work.
