It was military training schools I had in mind a moment ago.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
With further reference to the remarks of the leader of the opposition, I have had representations made to me in connection with cases which are similar to the one he quoted. I should like to give two illustrations. Just east of our town is a young man whose father is dead and who is working 150 acres all alone. He was called out for training, and I advised him to take the thirty-days training because there was a probability that it might be increased to four months. He had to hire someone to do the work of the farm. This boy is about twenty-four years of age and he put in his thirty days. Spring is now coming on; seeding will have to be taken care of, and then there will be the harvest later on. It seems to me that in a case like this it is just too bad to take this boy off the farm.
The other case I have in mind is that of a young man just north of our town. His father was in hospital for two or three months and has not been and will not be able to do anything because he has a severe case of diabetes. There are two boys, one twenty-one years of age and the other seventeen. They had to take the younger boy out of collegiate on account of a heart condition. The result was that there was only the one boy to work the farm. I took this ease up with the department here and with Mr. Martin, the divisional registrar, and I must say that the case received kind consideration.
These two cases are representative of many others throughout the country. In these days when farmers are having a difficult time, when they can hardly get any labour, it seems a
hardship that young men like these should be taken from the farms under the present trying circumstances. I am glad the leader of the opposition brought this matter to the attention of the committee, because I had intended to make representations when this question was up. Some provision should be.-made to look after cases of this kind.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am in hearty agreement with the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Golding), as well as with the representations which were made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). It seems to me that it would be a hardship for young men who are the only persons on farms to be taken at any time. There are large sections of Ontario where the work of the farm is just about as great in the winter as it is in the summer. This is true of dairying or any other type of farming where live stock is kept. The work of caring for live stock is increased in the winter when the stock must be kept in the stables. The minister should give serious consideration to providing complete exemption for these young men.
If they are taken away from the farm for any length of time, it will mean a serious loss in farm production. We have been told that farm production is necessary for the winning of the war, and I believe it is. The time is coming, and not far distant, when we shall need increased supplies of all kinds from the Canadian farmers. Again I ask the minister to give serious consideration to exempting all young men who are bona fide farmers and who are alone on farms.
While I am on my feet I should like to refer to the suggestion offered the other day by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterbor-ough (Mr. White), that it might be wise to set up boards of exemption to be headed by county judges. If a number of these boys are called up on any particular date, there is likely to be congestion before boards sitting in the military districts. The boys from my particular locality will have to apply to the board in Toronto, and undoubtedly there will be a large number asking, for exemption. If there is congestion, it will mean that the boys will have to wait for some time before their cases are heard. I cannot see why the county judge, who is impartial and should be fair, could not be vested with authority to say whether a postponement or an exemption should be granted. I leave this to the minister's discretion.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Under the regulations as now drafted it is not necessary that a man should appear in person. He may make his request in writing. In all probability, if a man has a bona fide case and presents it in
War Appropriation Bill

writing, his training will be postponed for the one call. He may be asked to prove his position before the second or third month, but the first call would likely be postponed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It seems to me that a difficulty would arise there. There would still be congestion as each case would have to be considered on its merits. A boy might wait until the last day before he is to go to training camp in order to hear from the division where his case was being considered. He would not know whether to hire someone to take his place, if it was possible to hire anyone, and he might have to leave the next morning without having made provision to carry on the work of the farm.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I had a case in my office quite recently. The minister will remember that within eight days of the call a young man is supposed to apply for exemption if that is desired. This particular young man had sole charge of a small farm, with a small herd of cattle. He was called for service and he got exemption. There were eight days within which, if his exemption was not granted, he would have to make arrangements for someone else to operate the farm. The uncertainty causes a great deal of hardship where there is only one man to manage the farm. He may be the only son of a farmer. I think advance notice of at least a month should be given so that a young man, if he is not granted exemption, can make arrangements for having his farm looked after while he is undergoing military training. I would urge that there be a little more certainty in this regard so far as calling farmers' sons is concerned.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Are any of the exempted classes being called and used in other work than soldiering? I refer to the Mennonites, the Doukhobors and so on. Are they being called up and used in some war effort?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Up to date there has been no call other than the military one. This question came up during the thirty-day training period. The Mennonites, for example, had asked that some means be found whereby they could perform a service to the state, which they asked the privilege of doing, but it was thought best to leave that matter until the question of a longer training period which was then being considered had been decided. Now that this question has been decided, there are provisions written into the regulations making possible the setting up of other methods of training and other methods of service which may be helpful in the prosecution of the war in which these persons may be engaged. I cannot give the details at the 
moment because the matter is being worked out with these people at the present time, but later on we shall probably have something to suggest in regard to it.
With regard to the period of eight days within which the young man will know whether his training is going to be postponed or not, after all there are only thirty or thirty-one days in a month and 6,000 calls are being made each month, so the month is pretty well divided up between the time of notice for medical examination, the time after medical examination and the time they are supposed to apply for postponement. Therefore I do not see how we could extend the time very much beyond the eight days and be able to carry on from month to month.
I would, however, say this, that as soon as the terms of the regulations are known, every individual has an opportunity at least to find out what they are, and these discussions here from time to time will perhaps enlighten them more or less with regard to what is expected. One does not need to wait until he is called in order to get full information with regard to the whole matter. A man can apply for postponement immediately after his medical examination, or even before medical examination. I do not think there is anything to prevent that. At all events, immediately after the medical examination they can send in their application indicating their position. That would speed up the time within which a reply could be received from the board. I do not, however, see how we could extend the time very much beyond what is allowed now.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Could notice not be sent out sixty days ahead?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Everyone who is
approaching twenty-one years of age has his notice now that he is likely to be called at any time. We call first those who were twenty-one last July. The next group is those who were twenty-one last August. The next group is those who were twenty-one last September, and so on. Therefore every young man who reads the newspapers or the regulations knows when he is likely to be called.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Could a man
not get notice on April 1 that he was to report for training on June 1?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
No. The young men
who became twenty-one last July, and a sufficient number of those who became twenty-one last August to make up a total of 6,000 men, would get their notice to report on the 20th of March. The next group would begin

War Appropriation Bill
from there, going on through August, September and so forth, taking the different age groups.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I should like to say just a
word about farmers' sons attending camp and the difficulties occasionally experienced. Out of some 2,200 men who went through my camp I had probably half a dozen to twenty cases which might be called serious ones. The trouble with most of them was that the men had not applied early enough for postponement of training. If they had applied for postponement as soon as they received their notice, it could probably have been arranged, but they left it until it was nearly time for them to report at the training centre and then it was too late for the board to arrange for substitutes to take their place. One department concerned has to supply a certain number of men for training and the other department has to train them. Therefore, when a man leaves his application for postponement to the very last minute, it is impossible for the board to notify other men to take their place and fill up the 750, or 1,000, or whatever may be the number required. I would suggest to the department that it might be well to send out their notices a little earlier and at the same time advise these men that if they wish to apply for postponement, they should apply immediately. In that way much of the difficulty would be obviated.
There are other cases that come up during training. The father, or a brother who has been left at home to look after the farm, may become sick and a request be made that the young man be released from the training camp and be sent home to look after the farm. That happens quite frequently. When the case is properly presented to the authorities, I can state that there is very little difficulty in having the man sent home. He is given credit for the time he has spent in training, and he will come back at some later date to complete his training.
I do not like to quote individual cases, but the most extreme one I had was that of a young man who had left his brother at home to look after the farm, with a housekeeper. His mother and father were dead, and the brother who was left at home had infantile paralysis. The housekeeper, who was not a young person, felt that she could not look after this invalid brother and the stock as well, and she left in the middle of winter. The chap with the infantile paralysis tried to look after seven head of cattle, some hogs and a couple of horses. I got word from a neighbour of his that this invalid man was dragging himself around on his hands, trying
to get water for the stock and looking after the pigs and cows, and he wanted to know if something could not be done to release the brother immediately. I took upon myself the responsibility of releasing the man and notified military headquarters at Saint John, and they approved what I had done. There is not as much difficulty, when these cases are taken up, as sometimes we might think there would be.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister about one particular case I have in mind. He stated that the young men who were twenty-one last July or August are being called up in the first draft. He also stated that postponement will be allowed in certain cases where it is considered necessary. If those postponements go through the next two training periods, the man will be over twenty-one; he may be twenty-two or more before he is called up. What will happen in a case of that kind? Will he still be called after he reaches the aige of twenty-two?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: When once he is called, he is subject to call any time later. The postponement may be, in some instances for a definite time; in others, it may be with power to call him at any time. He may not be called for a year and a half if he is working in some particular industry, but he is always subject to call.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It is not wise, I suppose, to generalize from isolated instances such as have been presented here to-day by myself or others. I wonder, however, whether the minister, in giving this matter consideration-and I know he and his officials must have given grave consideration to the principle upon which this draft is made- has definitely barred out the principle of selectivity. It seems to me that the door should not be barred to a change, having regard to the fact that the war effort, especially the industrial war effort, of the country is increasing in tempo all the time. I invite the minister and his advisers to give attention to incorporating in their regulations the adaptation of the principle of selectivity which obtains in other jurisdictions.
We have been dealing with isolated cases of farmers' sons, or where there is an only son, or where the son is head of the family, and so on. I suggest to the minister that some people should stay on the farm, and some people should stay in industry. Unless there is an invasion of Canada there are those who should definitely remain at their jobs, while others of a different category of age and so forth can much more easily be spared for the defence of the country and should take on this army training. I have thought that
War Appropriation Bill

the principle is too rigid, confined as it is to a particular class, and without any attention being paid to exceptions unless in cases where we are said to be under contract, if I may use that expression, with particular communities, communities of religious thought, or with conscientious objectors-and I include them in the same category. Would the minister say whether the principle of selectivity has been definitely abandoned? I think it is a fair method and it is followed in other jurisdictions.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
If by selectivity the
hon. member means the drawing of lots, or anything of that kind, as to what person should be called-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No; I am not speaking of that.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I would say that we are not making use of it. I would not say that it is not being considered or not being thought of. The same thing might be said to be true if the suggestion is that, let us say, all agriculturists engaged in a certain way in farming should be exempt. In that sense we have not accepted the theory that selectivity should apply. To the extent, however, that a person's time of training might be postponed because he is engaged in a certain industry, particularly in a seasonal industry, or that the time of service might be postponed because he is at present engaged in something essential to the prosecution of the war, that is some manufacturing industry, to that extent there is selection. That is, instructions are, through the regulations, being given to the boards which are sitting that certain things are to be done which would result in a selection being made, leaving some persons working at industries which are regarded as important, and taking others for training, for the time being. In that sense the selective element enters into what is being done.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That is
quite a limited sphere.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I would say it is limited.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
With regard to
choosing this number of 6,000 a month, will the choice be made in direct proportion to the population of the several provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It is made in proportion to the number of twenty-one year olds, or whatever class is being called, that the registration shows to be in that district; that is, in relation to the number desired by the Department of National Defence. The department ask us for so many men for a certain camp in a specified military district. We then

try to find the numbers there are in certain regions of that district, and divide up proportionately in those different areas.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I should like to
know something with respect to these exempt classes to which reference was made some little while ago. I noted that, when the minister replied, he referred only to the Mennonites and to the willingness which they had expressed to be of assistance in the war effort in other phases than those which are directly military. I noted, however, that he made no reference to the Doukhobors, and they constitute a problem in Saskatchewan, as well as further west, which to-day is causing considerable unrest. Have the Doukhobors made representations to the minister's department that they will not serve under any circumstances, regardless of the call which may be given to them, even though such service be connected only with the construction of roads and work of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: In making reference a few moments ago to the Mennonites, I did so because, before anyone, I believe, had made a suggestion that they should accept training, the Mennonites themselves intimated that they desired to have some sort of training provided for them. I believe they went so far as to say they were prepared to attend at camps and take training in first aid and ambulance work, indicating that they had no objection whatever to facing danger, that they were prepared to go into no-man's land or anywhere else and do a service for the country, provided they were not asked to kill. That is, they do not desire to take human life, or their belief is that under no circumstances should they take human life; but, short of that, they have no objections whatever to serving in any way the country desires them to serve, and they are willing to undergo any kind of training. They went even further than that; they said, "We are prepared to give free of charge to the state an equal term of employment." I believe they intimated, when we were using the thirty-day plan, that they were prepared to give two days for one, that is sixty days' labour to the state, in any work we liked to put them at, and that without any charge to the government. I mentioned the Mennonites because of the liberality, if I might use that expression, of the Mennonite people in making offers to do other things, since they object to military service itself.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Has that offer been accepted?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
We are trying to work out a plan. There is objection to having work
done gratis for the government at a time

War Appropriation Bill
when some people are unemployed, but possibly there is not an objection to using these men to get the camps ready and do other work of that kind which is needed in connection with the training itself, and we are trying now to work out plans in that direction.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Would you organize labour battalions and give them the same pay as the soldiers?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
They are not concerned about the pay. We probably would if we put them in, but they have not stipulated pay of any kind.
In dealing with the Doukhobors the problem is a little different; as far as I know, they did not come forward with an offer of that kind. Recently some inquiry has been made as to whether something might be done which would be satisfactory; whether the inquiry came first from the Doukhobors or began in our office I am not certain. There has, however, been correspondence between our office and the organization of Doukhobors along similar lines, that is, to find out what their attitude would be to service of that kind, and I am informed that a very considerable number of them are prepared to take part in similar training, or similar service. It is true there is a small proportion of the Doukhobor people, taking the numbers in western Canada as a whole, whom we shall probably find difficulty in getting to accede to any part of our regulations without some trouble. I do not know just what the final outcome will be, but at the moment we are negotiating in the hope that it will finally result in as nearly as possible one hundred per cent of both Menno-nites and Doukhobors being satisfied to take on some kind of training.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Are there any conscientious objectors in Canada apart from these groups that have been mentioned?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, but the number is comparatively small.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Are they being made use of?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Not up to the moment, but they would be subject to the same kind of thing.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What are the provisions for dealing with conscientious objectors?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The regulations as
drafted now are on exactly the same terms as the British. We did have different regulations for a time, but we found in practice that they do not work satisfactorily except in the form the British now have them drafted; that is, if a person claims to be a conscientious objector and can pretty well establish the fact, that is accepted.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: When a boy is called up for a medical examination and is classed as C, would he be accepted? Can the minister state the basis of the classification?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I assume it is a matter of health. There is no one called for training below Cl. Classes A, B and C are called up; we require them all in order to furnish the number necessary for the camp.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Exactly what state of health is indicated by class Cl; how bad would a man's health have to be in order to be classified as Cl? Would he have to be below normal in eyesight? Would a man who had to wear very strong glasses be called up, or would he be classified as Cl?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I think I shall have to let some of the military men answer that question, either that or bring in the exact schedules on which the examinations are made. I am told that glasses are all right.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Glasses are not all right in the navy.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I will place the exact schedules on the table.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Mennonites and Doukhobors have been mentioned; in what class are the Hutterites?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They are in a different group from the Doukhobors and Mennonites in that I do not think they have any legal rights to exemption in Canada, but they are conscientious objectors in the matter of military service, their beliefs being very much the same as those of the Mennonites and Doukhobors.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I realize the difficulty the minister has in connection with the Doukhobors and Mennonites, but I trust the government, in their desire for unity, will not lean too far back and cause more unrest among our own people, because I can tell him that the Doukhobors in British Columbia are the only group I know of that successfully defied the laws of this country, and got away with it. When a law is passed and regulations are put into effect, those regulations and that law should be enforced, irrespective of who is concerned, even if it causes a little fuss.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The statement of the minister regarding the attitude of the Mennonites should not pass without comment. Their offer to seek training in any line of military endeavour-except of course the necessity to kill-is deserving of commendation. They are willing to go to the front lines and serve as stretcher-bearers or in the medical corps, and for that they deserve credit, because

War Appropriation Bill

these people were admitted to Canada, I believe in 1873, under an agreed upon exemption from military service. We believe now that this was a mistake. I feel quite sure that the laws of Canada should demand of all her citizens that they be available for the defence of the country if the necessity arises. I feel confident that the younger generation of the Mennonites have the same idea and are willing to fulfil their obligations. We have quite a few Mennonites in my riding and quite a number of Hutterites, and I know a number of citizens of other races in my riding do object to seeing able-bodied men of this racial group who have come to Canada to make their home, staying at home and enjoying perhaps some increase of prosperity while other Canadians go and fight their battles. The very fact that the Mennonites have offered to do something in this war is a good omen and they should be encouraged to do more. I believe that the government should in future adopt the policy of not exempting any group from taking up the obligations that they owe to the state.
I was pleased to hear the minister say what he did for the sake of the Mennonites who reside in my constituency, and I wish to add my word of commendation that they have offered their services in this time of need.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I wish to refer briefly to some remarks made by the hon, member for Peterborough West with respect to the operation and production of the munition plant at Lindsay. On two occasions I believe that the hon. member has spoken disparagingly with regard to the production and operation at this plant. The first occasion was in the first session of this parliament on May 30 last, as reported on page 384 of Hansard of 1940. I was reviewing the production there, and he remarked that at the Lindsay plant they were only producing brass sheets. I had to correct that statement and the point I want to emphasize is that the source of the hon. member's information at that time was unreliable.
Then, as reported at page 873 of Hansard of this session the hon. member referred to a statement by one of the aldermen of Lindsay, as reported in the Peterborough Examiner, and went on to say, "It is patronage of the worst kind." The only reference I desire to make to the statement of the alderman is that this plant has been in operation for approximately two years. In that time hardly a week has passed when I have not met or been in conversation with at least some members of the city council, and during that entire period I have not heard the slightest complaint from the council as a body, or from any member of the council, with regard to the operation of the plant. Further, at one council [Mr. Leader 1
meeting which I attended the mayor was kind enough to say that I had not broken my word in connection with any pronouncement I had made regarding the production or the expected production at the munitions plant.
I want to emphasize that these suggestions of the hon. member reflect adversely upon two groups of officials. In the first place, they reflect upon the official in charge of the Lindsay office of the employment service of Canada. Hon. members who have given careful consideration to matters of this kind will, I am sure, agree that it is difficult to conceive of any position more difficult to fill than that of an employment officer, selecting men to be employed in any industry. That applies particularly where there is a large surplus of applicants for work; where, as in this case, few of those applying had any experience in the metal trades, which meant that a large number of applicants would come under the same classification. Perhaps there would be five or ten applicants for every job to be filled, and I am sure no official could administer work of that kind without disappointing someone. I should think that would be inevitable.
The other group of officials upon whom this suggestion reflects adversely are the superintendent and those associated with him in the administration and management of the plant. A great many of these men have been with the Department of National Defence for a long period of years, associated in various ways with the production and inspection of munitions. Latterly, of course, they have been in the employ of the Department of Munitions and Supply. These officials have had to perform a most trying and difficult task. In the first place, a government plant must do a certain amount of pioneering and experimentation with new machines and improvements on old machines. I am sure these officials have given freely of their skill, patience and perseverance and have put in very long hours, with a great deal of overtime, in an endeavour to produce munitions of the highest possible quality.
Just in that connection I should like to refer to the conferences I had with the senior officials of the Department of National Defence during the early negotiations leading to the reopening and putting into production of that plant. I am sure the present Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), who at that time was Minister of National Defence, would agree that at those conferences and in those negotiations many difficulties were encountered in connection with this production. Some of the officials referred to the work done in that plant during the last war. I recall

one high ranking official who took no pains to hide his disgust, though that may be putting it too strongly, at the results obtained in that plant at that time. From the beginning of the negotiations with regard to that plant it was my greatest desire, as I stated time and again, that the production should be of the highest quality, in order that our men at the front might be backed up with the very best type of munitions.

In the speech which I made on November 12 I did not condemn the scheme. I pointed out what I thought were the weaknesses, but I pointed out also what I thought were some of the advantages. I did that on eye-witness evidence, and in the belief that I should bring it forward in this house. My colleague did the same thing. He did not condemn the plan in toto; he said it served a useful purpose and he was rather proud of some of the men and the advance that they had made.
I suggest to the minister that it must have been known to him soon after the scheme was put into operation that the training was wholly inadequate for the primary purpose of the defence of Canada. Upon trial it was found that the limited training period was not long enough to prepare these men to be put into the field against a well-trained and disciplined enemy. There were reasons for that. In the
first place the syllabus was too crowded, being based upon a seven and a half hour day for twenty-two of the thirty days. The daily Syllabus comprised ten forty-five minute periods. There was a total of 220 periods with a five minute rest allowed between periods. The syllabus provided for drill, gas, bayonet, rifle, field craft, road marches, military education, physical training and anti-aircraft work. Spare periods were also included, and all these items were taught within the short space of 220 forty-minute periods. In other words, each trainee was given about 146 working hours of instruction, less what he spent on fatigue or picket duty or in the hospital. That last item became very important during the last training period because of the prevalence of flu. This was nobody's fault, of course.
It was found that the average recruit or trainee could not properly absorb all the material in the short space of time allowed. To spend more time on each subject would cut down the period of training and consequently fail to achieve even an approximate basic training. Therefore, there was no alternative but to lengthen the period of training. When the defects of the crowded training period became apparent, I think I was among the first to suggest the lengthening of the period. I should like to refer to a statement I made in this connection on November 12, during the debate on the address. At that time I made some very constructive suggestions which were offered after discussion with some of the best military men in Canada. These men had examined the matter without prejudice and in the light of a desire to do the best under the circumstances for these trainees and in the belief that we were not getting value for our money. I intend to deal with that phase of the matter at a later time. I then went on to say:
After giving the matter the best consideration I can, and having obtained the best advice I can, I am going to make two concrete suggestions. I hope the minister will give heed to them, because these suggestions are offered in the best of good faith, designed to achieve an objective which I think both he and I have at heart.
The first suggestion is that the length of time of training for these men be increased to at least four months, and that we train three groups a year instead of ten. The first eight weeks of this four months' course should be designated the basic recruits' course, and the second eight weeks the trained men's weeks, and graduation being required from one course into the other.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: This expert purchaser?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes. I will give the minister the name if he wants to know. I prefer not to put it on record, but I will tell him who he is and what firm employs him. He bought at least 280,000 feet of these boards from Mr. H. J. Mackenzie, life insurance agent of the town of Truro, who is represented to me to have been the campaign manager of the hon. member for Colchester. If the hon. member says that is not true, I accept his word absolutely. But he was not a producer, and as far as I know he did not have a dollar's interest in a lumber mill in the county of Colchester.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit me? Of course, it is not in my department, and I have not heard either of the names before: I have not yet heard the name of the lumber buyer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I will give the minister the name of the lumber buyer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I would be interested to know why this lumber buyer would go to an insurance agent to purchase.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: So would we-absolutely. I should like to know how he got in touh with Mackenzie.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I thought he was given
a certificate of character.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes. Because of the pressure on him to get the stuff in; he could not get it from the big mills in New Brunswick; he could not wait. It was the old story of "Cox can't wait." Perhaps my hon. friend knows that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes. Who was the lumber buyer?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The lumber buyer was a Mr. McCabe of Campbell, MacLaurin Lumber company.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: And he was a Conservative candidate in Toronto.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I never
heard of his being a candidate. I have not any idea of his politics.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: He was also president of a Conservative association.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I hope so. I know his principal is a first-class Conservative; and he gave this man's services to the timber controller at the timber controller's request, and he operated without a dollar of expense to this government.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
This looks like collusion
between the Grits and the Tories. It is a "fishy" deal.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Perhaps it is. May I ask the hon. member for Colchester if any of his production went into those camps through Mr. H. J. Mackenzie. I do not know, but I am not debarred from asking that question.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I ask the right to answer that question here and now. Not one stick.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I accept the hon. gentleman's statement without question. I make no charge. I do not know. But I have the right to ask that question.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not think you have.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Have I not the right to say what I did this afternoon?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Surely.
The hon. member has the right to say anything he wants to say in this chamber, so long as he does not violate the rules of the house. And I have the right to criticize what he has to say. Let me proceed.
To come back to the general principles, the cost of the camps was greatly increased because of the pressure of the national defence departments to get these camps built in order that they might be put in operation. If there had

War Appropriation Bill
been proper business administration, these camps could have been built at a saving to the country of from one-fourth to one-third.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That would have meant
some delay, and that would have been "red tape" then.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Possibly
it would. Of course, we always leave an avenue open.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It would have been "red tape."

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I do not
know any people who ought to know more about red tape than the representative of the defence departments.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But I say that if all this business care had been taken, it would have been characterized as red tape.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not think so. I believe that the tender principle in this country is still a good, sound, safe principle, even in war time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I thought the man who
purchased was a man who could himself purchase. I did not know that the hon. gentleman suggested that the man who purchased was not a good buyer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The minister has got his wires crossed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What did the hon. gentleman talk about the tenders for?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I spoke of tenders for the construction of these buildings. Perhaps it is my fault that I did not make it clear. I would not suggest for a moment that the minister's mind was obtuse; that would not be fair.
Coming back for a moment to the construction of these camps, to tell me that the camp at Fredericton cost $254,000 is to advertise to this country government incompetence and government waste, and I believe that an analysis of the whole break-down will reveal it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend will have a full opportunity to show it if he can.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am
taking the opportunity. I am under no obligation to the minister for that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend thinks that taking up time at this stage, at the tail-end of the week, to bring up these matters, with no chance to reply, is taking a proper opportunity, when he knows that there is a committee on expenses going into these very matters?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I think I am entitled to take my own time and my own method to make my presentation. I notice the government does not give very much consideration when they want to make a presentation. They seize time by the forelock; they take whatever time they want, and we are not to be denied the like privilege.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Nobody is denying any
privilege. I am only saying that this is not the right way. If my hon. friend thinks this is the way in the public interest to investigate these matters, nobody is stopping him.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The public are talking about this. My whole city is seething about the cost of these thirty-day training units.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is because the hon. gentleman lives there.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I could
give the hon. gentleman a lot more. Who was put in charge of the construction?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I cannot tell my hon.
friend.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The Liberal zone captain in the city of Fredericton was put in charge of the construction, and he had the hiring of these men. Hon. members can imagine what happened. I will give the minister his name if he wants it. His name is Hayward Allan.
We have already dealt, sufficiently I think, with the question of the defects in the medical examination. That was discussed here on a previous occasion, and I must say that the number rejected after they got to the training centre seemed to me very large. I do not, however, think any blame can be laid on the department for that. The defect was that there was not uniformity in the preliminary medical examinations. I do not believe that the doctors who examined these men were fully instructed. The result was that a large percentage were rejected when they came to the medical board at the training centre. That may have been inevitable. One should not be dogmatic about that unless one has satisfactory proof of the facts, which I have not.
I am not going to take up the third defect of the thirty-day training scheme, connected with the question of withdrawal of men from essential war industries. We have debated that subject quite sufficiently, and I believe that the regulations, if they are to be put into effect, will provide satisfactorily for noninterference with war industry. The only argument that I can draw from that, and the recommendation I make, would be that there
War Appropriation Bill

should be some form of selective draft so as not to interfere with war industry or with the farm boy who cannot be spared.
I suggest that another defect of the scheme was-and this will be rectified in a measure by the four months' scheme-that it was too expensive, with a constant turnover of men. Partly to train a man and then return him to civilian life where he would forget all about this very preliminary training was unsound. The better plan would have been to complete his course entirely and then absorb him into the active army.
The plan for the future provides that the twenty-one-year-old class will be called up for training and the call will be confined to them. Six thousand will be called up the middle of this month-I think the call is out now and they will be on hand next week- and 6,000 each succeeding month; then there will be a rotation. These men will all receive basic training for two months. After this they can volunteer for service in any branch of the army, navy or air force for service overseas if openings are available, otherwise *they will be retained for a further two months for specialized training in one or other of the branches of the army. Some of these young men will be taken into the active army at the end of the first two months if they wish to enlist. But there is no obligation.
I suggest to the minister in all frankness that that is a real defect in the system. He might give consideration to remedying that defect as time goes on. I am sure he is of the same mind as I am. If he cannot give effect to that principle now, will he take it into consideration and possibly at a later stage in the war give effect to it?-because I believe that should be done.
I shall not go further into this aspect of the matter, but there is one other point to which I should like to refer. The minister has partly cleared it up in the statement about the officers' training courses that are to be set up. During the present break period instructional staffs in the various centres should I think have been given a uniform course of advanced training. The young men who went into the training centres as instructors were very keen, but they themselves had had only a limited training course, because, owing to the drain, that had been placed upon our instructional staff for the overseas divisions, they were new men. I think at one time I suggested to the minister that it might be good policy for the department to bring back from England some of the non-commissioned officers and other

trained men, and it may be that partial effect has been given to that principle. But there was a great weakness in the system because the officers themselves knew little beyond the syllabus of the thirty day plan. They were new men as a rule-some of course were older; all they had had themselves was partial training over a period of two or three weeks, and what they could gather night by night by the most intensive study-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend is wrong about that; they were not new men.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Well a great many of them were new men. The minister says categorically they were not new men; I tell him many of them were new men in the work of instruction.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The way my hon. friend
puts it, it sounds as if they were brought in off the street.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
No, the minister knows better than that. I did not say that, and it was no proper inference to take from what I said. These staffs of instructors consisted for the most part of officers and non-commissioned officers from the non-permanent active militia units. Their training was limited. Anyone knows how much training the non-permanent active militia had before the war. It was negligible. There could not be proper training. It is of no use to harp on that now; it is past and gone, and no one in particular is responsible-we just felt that we could not afford it. In the light of after events we see now that it was a mistake, but none of us have at a given time all the vision we ought to have in respect to what may happen in the future.
It is suggested that there should be set up between periods not only these officer training schools that the minister has I think very properly intimated will be established, one at Brockville and one in the west, but also schools at various centres for the training of the non-commissioned officers. My information is that these after all are the men who do the actual work of instructing and training under the supervision of an officer. I may be wrong, but I do not think the officers themselves are the actual instructors. I understand the instruction is given by the noncommissioned officers under the supervision of the officers. There ought to be more intensification of their instruction in order that they may be able to instruct the trainee. Whether we have enough trained instructors among the non-commissioned officers in these training camps to proceed with a four months'

Questions
syllabus I do not know, but I am informed that we have not. If we have not, the matter should be rectified, and I have no doubt it is receiving attention from those in authority.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I propose on Monday to give a statement in answer to what the hon. member for Vancouver South has said. I should like very much to accept the invitation of the hon. member to give a short statement with regard to the object of this training.
I regret that the leader of the opposition thought fit to bring these matters up, particularly with regard to the purchase of lumber, and so forth, in the absence of my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I shall endeavour, however, to get information about that also and give it to the committee on Monday.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Ilsley the house adjourned at 6 p.m.
Monday, March 17, 1941.
